Pycroft's petrel (Pterodroma pycrofti) is a small gadfly petrel endemic to the New Zealand region. Nestlings attain an asymptotic body mass of 250 grams [Wwi = 250 grams] prior to fledging, representing the ultimate wet weight reached during the nestling period. This substantial increase from the comparatively modest mass at hatching reflects the efficiency of parental provisioning in this species. During the incubation period, eggs maintained under controlled thermal conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days], an incubation duration that is relatively brief for a procellariiform seabird. This abbreviated developmental timeline may be an adaptation to the relatively cool, stable temperatures of the burrow environment, where thermal variability is minimal compared to surface nests, thereby accelerating embryonic development within the constraints of a limited food supply for the attending adult. The observed incubation temperature aligns closely with the optimal range for embryonic growth in closely related Pterodroma species, ensuring high hatching success in the temperate climate of the breeding islands.

Field studies on the breeding biology of Pycroft's petrel have provided key data on reproductive rates in this species. Females typically lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and, given the protracted breeding season common to many Procellariiformes, raise only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This low annual reproductive output is a characteristic life-history trait among gadfly petrels, trading off high parental investment in a single offspring against the energetic constraints of foraging over vast oceanic distances. The limited reproductive rate is linked to the species' slow maturation and extended lifespan, which together buffer population numbers against periodic fluctuations in marine prey availability. Under the typical metabolic conditions of an incubating adult, which maintains a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] during extended incubation shifts, the energetic cost of producing that single egg is a significant portion of the female's annual energy budget.

The juvenile and adult life stages of Pycroft's petrel are characterized by specific developmental thresholds reached under a consistent internal body temperature. Under a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], nestlings achieve the ability to fledge, marking the completion of the dependent chick phase, at 80 days after hatching [tx = 80 days after hatching]. This milestone coincides with the full development of flight feathers and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to support the initial post-fledging foraging period at sea. Following fledging, young birds undergo a prolonged period of oceanic wandering before returning to natal colonies to breed. The transition to reproductive maturity is delayed considerably, with the onset of puberty occurring at 240 days after hatching [tp = 240 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime, although this physiological maturation does not immediately translate into breeding activity, as young birds often require additional years to acquire the necessary foraging experience and secure a nesting site at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

Long-term banding studies have provided critical insights into the longevity and reproductive scheduling of Pycroft's petrel. Under free-ranging conditions, with adult birds maintaining a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] during their active periods, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 9,125 days [am = approximately 9,125 days], which corresponds to roughly 25 years. This remarkable longevity is typical of small procellariiform seabirds and is a direct correlate of their slow life-history pace, which includes deferred reproduction and low annual fecundity. The time elapsed between hatching and the successful production of a first brood is 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching] when birds are operating at a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This substantial delay between fledging and first breeding is a common pattern among oceanic seabirds, reflecting the time required to master complex foraging skills and to establish a territory within a dense breeding colony, where competition for suitable burrow sites is intense.

Comparative life-history data from related gadfly petrels offer a useful perspective for interpreting the growth parameters of Pycroft's petrel. For instance, hatchlings of the closely related Bonin petrel (Pterodroma hypoleuca), a species that occupies a similar ecological niche in the subtropical Pacific, are recorded with a wet weight at birth of 7.7 grams [Wwb = 7.7 grams]. While this value is measured in a congener, it serves as a valuable benchmark for understanding neonatal mass in the genus, given the similar body sizes and reproductive strategies shared between these two species. Pycroft's petrel, like many Procellariiformes, invests heavily in a single, relatively large egg that yields a well-developed neonate capable of thermoregulation within the first few days of life. This initial hatchling mass, though modest, supports the rapid growth trajectory necessary to achieve the ultimate nestling mass of 250 grams [Wwi = 250 grams] within the relatively short fledging period of 80 days after hatching [tx = 80 days after hatching], a developmental pace that requires consistent and high-quality provisioning from both parents at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].
